source.title: Data Scaling Laws for Radiology Foundation Models
source.authors: Maximilian Ilse; Harshita Sharma; A. Schwaighofer; Sam Bond-Taylor; F. Pérez-García; Olesya Melnichenko; Anne-Marie G. Sykes; K. Horst; Ashish Khandelwal; Maxwell C. Reynolds; M. Wetscherek; Noel C. F. Codella; J. Alvarez-Valle; Korfiatis Panagiotis; Valentina Salvatelli

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or truncation; the provided text contains the paper and appendix.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests data-scaling behavior in radiology vision encoders and reports both roughly power-law trends and departures from idealized scaling, including saturation and a reversed trend under domain shift. It is a refinement of the general scaling claim, not a language-model loss reproduction.
record.gate_note: The study varies the amount of continual pretraining data for vision encoders while holding model size and compute protocol fixed, then measures downstream radiology performance. These results bear on the broader scaling-form and downstream-predictability versions, but it does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, vary parameters or training compute to find compute-optimal allocations, or predict a larger run’s loss from smaller runs. Cited results from other papers are not recorded as rows. Detailed per-finding table entries and metadata-stratified comparisons are not scaling-curve results.
record.test_reason: Radiology vision encoders (MI2 360M, RAD-DINO 87M) are continually pretrained on nested subsets of 30k to 3.5M chest X-rays, with model size and compute protocol held fixed. The study fits f(x)=αx^k to downstream metrics against pretraining-data size. This is a new setting (image encoders, continual pretraining, downstream metrics) with results on whether data scaling stays power-law-like, so T3 fits better than T5. No language-model loss is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors claim clear data-scaling laws up to 3.5M samples but note that many curves deviate from ideal power laws: noisy at small data, plateauing at large data, and complicated by domain shift. MI2 is better on findings tasks and RAD-DINO on tube tasks; UniCL tube labels close MI2's gap. They also say the shallow slopes imply billions of samples to raise averages, so targeted data selection beats brute-force collection.
record.recipe_differences: Radiology vision encoders rather than language models; varies continual-pretraining dataset size while holding model size and compute protocol fixed; evaluates downstream classification, segmentation, and report-generation metrics rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy; no compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome changes with encoder approach, downstream task, and dataset/domain. MI2 and RAD-DINO have different findings-classification slopes; tube-label supervision changes MI2 performance; VinDR shows a reversed RAD-DINO trend; small-data segmentation is inconsistent; Incorrect Placement F1 saturates quickly.
record.problems: The study measures downstream task metrics rather than pretraining loss. Several scaling curves are reported only in figures without numerical values in the text. The VinDR benchmark is described as small and potentially domain-mismatched; segmentation trends are described as inconsistent below 100k samples. For report generation, only one MAIRA-2 model is trained per pretraining size and method; bootstrap CIs are used to estimate variability.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-finding and per-tube category results at 3.5M, and metadata-stratified findings comparisons, are omitted because they are not separate dataset-size scaling curves. Figures 2–5 provide the reported scaling sweeps; Table 1–5 contain additional task-level comparisons not individually extracted here.

untested.parts: No language models and no held-out pretraining loss. Parameters and compute are not varied.
No fitted law is validated against a much larger held-out run. The RAD-DINO segmentation 'extrapolation' is qualitative and unchecked.
Model size and compute allocation are not varied.
Architecture shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
Only downstream metrics are measured for image encoders under continual pretraining; no pretraining loss, video, or repeated-data regimes. Model-size scaling is not tested.
Downstream performance is related to pretraining-data size only, not to pretraining loss or model size.
Parameter counting, schedule and fitting-method choices are not varied. No compute-optimal split is studied.

missing.what: Per-task scaling curves for rib fracture AUPRC (MI2 3.5M is 6 points above OWM) and mediastinal drain AUPRC, showing larger gains than the averages.
DICE scaling curves for lines-and-tubes segmentation.
ROUGE-L and RadFact logical F1 at 3.5M vs open weights. RadFact for RAD-DINO shows no gain (63.0 vs 63.3), suggesting no data-scaling benefit on that metric.
Authors' statement that improving average performance may require billions of samples, implied by the shallow fitted slopes.

record.verdict_notes: All measures are downstream metrics against continual-pretraining data size from existing checkpoints; no loss, model-size or compute scaling is measured. Only R1–R3 have explicit fits, and no fit uncertainty is given. The 1M and 3.5M points use a single encoder each. Table 4's AVG column appears to duplicate the ETT column. V7 links were removed from rows that show neither exponent differences nor curve bending.

versions.untested_parts: No language models or held-out language-model pretraining loss are measured.
No extrapolation of language-model loss from smaller runs to much larger runs is tested.
Model size and compute-optimal parameter/token allocation are not varied or measured.
Architecture details are not systematically varied at fixed parameter count.

Tests image-based radiology encoders and continual pretraining data scaling, not video or other modalities, repeated-data regimes, or general fine-tuning and transfer regimes. The measured outcomes are downstream metrics, not pretraining loss.
Tests downstream classification, segmentation, and report-generation metrics against pretraining-data scale; does not test downstream performance against language-model pretraining loss.
Findings concern data-scale curves, tasks, encoder approaches, and domain shift. Parameter-counting choices, language-model training schedules, and compute-optimal splits are not tested.
